588	  /// Perform a collective-scoped matrix multiply-accumulate
589	  /// Producer Perspective
590	  template <
591	    class TensorA, class TensorB,
592	    class TensorSFA, class TensorSFB,
593	    class KTileIterator, class BlockCoord
594	  >
595	  CUTLASS_DEVICE void
596	  load(
597	      Params const& params,
598	      MainloopPipeline pipeline,
599	      PipelineState smem_pipe_write,
600	      cute::tuple<TensorA, TensorB, TensorSFA, TensorSFB> const& load_inputs,
601	      BlockCoord const& blk_coord,
602	      KTileIterator k_tile_iter, int k_tile_count,
603	      int thread_idx,
604	      uint32_t block_rank_in_cluster,
605	      TensorStorage& shared_tensors) {
606	    int lane_predicate = cute::elect_one_sync();
607	
608	    if (lane_predicate) {
609	
610	      Tensor sA = make_tensor(make_smem_ptr(shared_tensors.smem_A.begin()), SmemLayoutA{});        // (BLK_M,BLK_K,PIPE)
611	      Tensor sB = make_tensor(make_smem_ptr(shared_tensors.smem_B.begin()), SmemLayoutB{});        // (BLK_N,BLK_K,PIPE)
612	      Tensor sSFA = make_tensor(make_smem_ptr(shared_tensors.smem_SFA.begin()), SmemLayoutSFA{});  // (BLK_M,BLK_K,PIPE)
613	      Tensor sSFB = make_tensor(make_smem_ptr(shared_tensors.smem_SFB.begin()), SmemLayoutSFB{});  // (BLK_N,BLK_K,PIPE)
614	
615	      //
616	      // Prepare the TMA loads for A, B, SFA and SFB
617	      //
618	
619	      auto [gA_mkl, gB_nkl, gSFA_mkl, gSFB_nkl] = load_inputs;
620	
621	      auto block_tma_a = params.tma_load_a.get_slice(0);
622	      auto block_tma_b = params.tma_load_b.get_slice(0);
623	
624	      auto block_tma_sfa = params.tma_load_sfa.get_slice(0);
625	      auto block_tma_sfb = params.tma_load_sfb.get_slice(0);
626	
627	      // Partition the inputs based on the current block coordinates.
628	      auto [m_coord, n_coord, k_coord, l_coord] = blk_coord;
629	
630	      Tensor gA =   gA_mkl(_,_,m_coord,_,l_coord);                                                     // (BLK_M,BLK_K,k)
631	      Tensor gB =   gB_nkl(_,_,n_coord,_,l_coord);                                                     // (BLK_N,BLK_K,k)
632	      Tensor gSFA = gSFA_mkl(_,_,m_coord,_,l_coord);                                                   // (BLK_M,BLK_K,k)
633	      Tensor gSFB = gSFB_nkl(_,_,n_coord,_,l_coord);                                                   // (BLK_N,BLK_K,k)
634	
635	      // Partition source and destination tensors for tma copies
636	      Tensor tAgA = block_tma_a.partition_S(gA);                                              // (TMA,TMA_M,TMA_K,k)
637	      Tensor tAsA = block_tma_a.partition_D(sA);                                              // (TMA,TMA_M,TMA_K,PIPE)
638	
639	      Tensor tBgB = block_tma_b.partition_S(gB);                                              // (TMA,TMA_N,TMA_K,k)
640	      Tensor tBsB = block_tma_b.partition_D(sB);                                              // (TMA,TMA_N,TMA_K,PIPE)
641	
642	      Tensor tAgSFA = block_tma_sfa.partition_S(gSFA);                                        // (TMA,TMA_M,TMA_K,k)
643	      Tensor tAsSFA = block_tma_sfa.partition_D(sSFA);                                        // (TMA,TMA_M,TMA_K,PIPE)
644	
645	      Tensor tBgSFB = block_tma_sfb.partition_S(gSFB);                                        // (TMA,TMA_N,TMA_K,k)
646	      Tensor tBsSFB = block_tma_sfb.partition_D(sSFB);                                        // (TMA,TMA_N,TMA_K,PIPE)
647	
648	      // Mainloop
649	      CUTLASS_PRAGMA_NO_UNROLL
650	      for ( ; k_tile_count > 0; --k_tile_count) {
651	        // LOCK smem_pipe_write for _writing_
652	        pipeline.producer_acquire(smem_pipe_write);
653	
654	        //
655	        // Copy gmem to smem for *k_tile_iter
656	        //
657	
658	        using BarrierType = typename MainloopPipeline::ProducerBarrierType;
659	        BarrierType* tma_barrier = pipeline.producer_get_barrier(smem_pipe_write);
660	
661	        int write_stage = smem_pipe_write.index();
662	        copy(params.tma_load_a.with(*tma_barrier), tAgA(_,_,_,*k_tile_iter), tAsA(_,_,_,write_stage));
663	        copy(params.tma_load_b.with(*tma_barrier), tBgB(_,_,_,*k_tile_iter), tBsB(_,_,_,write_stage));
664	
665	        copy(params.tma_load_sfa.with(*tma_barrier), tAgSFA(_,_,_,*k_tile_iter), tAsSFA(_,_,_,write_stage));
666	        copy(params.tma_load_sfb.with(*tma_barrier), tBgSFB(_,_,_,*k_tile_iter), tBsSFB(_,_,_,write_stage));
667	
668	        // Advance k tile
669	        ++k_tile_iter;
670	        ++smem_pipe_write;
671	      }
672	    }
673	    __syncwarp();
674	  }
675	
676	  /// Perform a Producer Epilogue to prevent early exit of blocks in a Cluster
677	  CUTLASS_DEVICE void
678	  load_tail(MainloopPipeline pipeline, PipelineState smem_pipe_write) {
679	    int lane_predicate = cute::elect_one_sync();
680	
681	    // Issue the epilogue waits
682	    if (lane_predicate) {
683	      /* This helps avoid early exit of blocks in Cluster
684	       * Waits for all stages to either be released (all
685	       * Consumer UNLOCKs), or if the stage was never used
686	       * then would just be acquired since the phase was
687	       * still inverted from make_producer_start_state
688	       */
689	      pipeline.producer_tail(smem_pipe_write);
690	    }
691	  }

1	/*
2	Fast Dequantization (Converting INT4/INT8/FP4/FP8 to FP16/BF16)
3	
4	The process of fast dequantization can be summarized as a combination
5	of bitwise operations and floating-point computations:
6	
7	weight =>(bit_op / bitwise operations)=>
8	f16_value =>(flop / floating-point computation)=>
9	dequantized_weight
10	
11	Since the dequantized weights typically require subtracting the zero point and
12	applying a scale factor, the floating-point computation step can be fused with
13	the zero-point subtraction and scaling operations.
14	
15	The following are the parts that need to be modified for the fused operation
16	of zero-point subtraction and scaling.
17	
18	## INT4 => FP16/BF16 or INT8 => FP16
19	
20	The floating-point computation is `__hsub2`
21	
22	If has zero points:
23	
24	    flop(bit_op(weight)) - flop(bit_op(zp))
25	  = sub(bit_op(weight), bias) - sub(bit_op(zp), bias)
26	  = bit_op(weight) - bit_op(zp)
27	
28	so we don't need additional modification.
29	
30	If has float zero points:
31	
32	    flop(bit_op(weight)) - fzp
33	  = sub(bit_op(weight), bias) - fzp
34	  = bit_op(weight) - (fzp + bias)
35	
36	where the `fzp + bias` can be computed at weight loading. But this
37	may have accuracy issue, so we should not use this in most cases.
38	
39	If has not zero points:
40	
41	    scale(flop(bit_op(weight)))
42	  = scale(sub(bit_op(weight), bias))
43	  = scale(bit_op(weight)) - scale(bias)
44	  = fma(bit_op(weight), scale_factor, scale(bias))
45	
46	where the `scale(bias)` can be cached. But this may have accuracy issue,
47	so we should not use this in most cases.
48	
49	
50	## INT8 => BF16
51	
52	INT8 => BF16 is a special case, it use byte_perm instead of flop.
53	We cannot fused byte_perm with scaling.
54	
55	
56	## FP4/FP8 => FP16/BF16
57	
58	    scale(flop(bit_op(weight)))
59	  = scale(mul(bit_op(weight), multiplier))
60	  = mul(bit_op(weight), scale_factor * multiplier)
61	
62	where `scale_factor * multiplier` can be computed at weight loading.
63	
64	*/

71	// Lookup-table based 3-input logical operation; explicitly used for
72	// dequantization as the compiler does not seem to automatically recognize it in
73	// all cases.
74	template <int lut>
75	__device__ inline int lop3(int a, int b, int c) {
76	  int res;
77	  asm volatile("lop3.b32 %0, %1, %2, %3, %4;\n" : "=r"(res) : "r"(a), "r"(b), "r"(c), "n"(lut));
78	  return res;
79	}

81	// Constructs destination register by taking bytes from 2 sources (based on
82	// mask)
83	template <int start_byte, int mask>
84	__device__ inline uint32_t prmt(uint32_t a) {
85	  uint32_t res;
86	  asm volatile("prmt.b32 %0, %1, %2, %3;\n" : "=r"(res) : "r"(a), "n"(start_byte), "n"(mask));
87	  return res;
88	}

93	//
94	// Efficiently dequantize 4bit values packed in an int32 value into a full
95	// B-fragment of 4 fp16 values. We mostly follow the strategy in the link below,
96	// with some small changes:
97	// - FP16:
98	// https://github.com/NVIDIA/FasterTransformer/blob/release/v5.3_tag/src/fastertransformer/cutlass_extensions/include/cutlass_extensions/interleaved_numeric_conversion.h#L215-L287
99	// - BF16:
100	// https://github.com/NVIDIA/FasterTransformer/blob/release/v5.3_tag/src/fastertransformer/cutlass_extensions/include/cutlass_extensions/interleaved_numeric_conversion.h#L327-L385
101	//
102	template <>
103	__device__ inline void dequant<half2, sglang::kU4B8.id(), true>(int q, half2* frag_b) {
104	  const int MASK = 0x000f000f;
105	  const int EX = 0x64006400;
106	  // Guarantee that the `(a & b) | c` operations are LOP3s.
107	  int lo = lop3<(0xf0 & 0xcc) | 0xaa>(q, MASK, EX);
108	  q >>= 4;
109	  int hi = lop3<(0xf0 & 0xcc) | 0xaa>(q, MASK, EX);
110	
111	  frag_b[0] = *reinterpret_cast<half2*>(&lo);
112	  frag_b[1] = *reinterpret_cast<half2*>(&hi);
113	}
114	
115	template <>
116	__device__ inline void dequant<half2, sglang::kU4B8.id(), false>(int q, half2* frag_b) {
117	  const int LO = 0x000f000f;
118	  const int HI = 0x00f000f0;
119	  const int EX = 0x64006400;
120	  // Guarantee that the `(a & b) | c` operations are LOP3s.
121	  // clang-format off
122	  int lo = lop3<(0xf0 & 0xcc) | 0xaa>(q, LO, EX);
123	  int hi = lop3<(0xf0 & 0xcc) | 0xaa>(q, HI, EX);
124	  // clang-format on
125	  // We want signed int4 outputs, hence we fuse the `-8` symmetric zero point
126	  // directly into `SUB` and `ADD`.
127	  const int SUB = 0x64086408;
128	  const int MUL = 0x2c002c00;
129	  const int ADD = 0xd480d480;
130	  frag_b[0] = __hsub2(*reinterpret_cast<half2*>(&lo), *reinterpret_cast<const half2*>(&SUB));
131	  frag_b[1] = __hfma2(
132	      *reinterpret_cast<half2*>(&hi), *reinterpret_cast<const half2*>(&MUL), *reinterpret_cast<const half2*>(&ADD));
133	}

469	  frag_b[1] = *reinterpret_cast<const half2*>(&Out1);
470	  frag_b[0] = *reinterpret_cast<const half2*>(&Out2);
471	};
472	
473	template <>
474	__device__ inline void dequant_fp8_scales<nv_bfloat162, sglang::kFE4M3fn.id()>(int q, nv_bfloat162* frag_b) {
475	  constexpr int FP8_EXPONENT = 4, BF16_EXPONENT = 8;
476	  constexpr int RIGHT_SHIFT = BF16_EXPONENT - FP8_EXPONENT;
477	  constexpr int MASK = 0x7F007F00;
478	
479	  // Extract and shift FP8 values to BF16 format
480	  int Out1 = ((q & 0x80008000) >> 1) | ((q & MASK) >> RIGHT_SHIFT);
481	  q <<= 8;
482	  int Out2 = ((q & 0x80008000) >> 1) | ((q & MASK) >> RIGHT_SHIFT);
483	
484	  // Note: reverse indexing is intentional because weights are permuted
485	  frag_b[1] = *reinterpret_cast<const nv_bfloat162*>(&Out1);
486	  frag_b[0] = *reinterpret_cast<const nv_bfloat162*>(&Out2);
487	}
488	
489	template <>
490	__device__ inline void dequant_fp8_scales<nv_bfloat162, sglang::kFE8M0fnu.id()>(int q, nv_bfloat162* frag_b) {
491	  // In this conversion, 2 ** -127 in FP8E8M0 would become 0 in BF16,
492	  // but we assume that such a extreme value would not occur in real models.
493	  int Out1 = (q & 0xFF00FF00) >> 1;
494	  q <<= 7;
495	  int Out2 = q & 0x7F807F80;
496	
497	  // Note: reverse indexing is intentional because weights are permuted
498	  frag_b[1] = *reinterpret_cast<const nv_bfloat162*>(&Out1);
499	  frag_b[0] = *reinterpret_cast<const nv_bfloat162*>(&Out2);
500	}
501	
502	#endif
503	
504	}  // namespace MARLIN_NAMESPACE_NAME
505

> AGENT

关键发现：`dequant_fp8_scales<nv_bfloat162>` 实际上**已经包含**了 sign bit 重定位（`>>1`）+ mantissa 移位（`>>4`），这是 FP8 E4M3 (bias 7) → BF16 (bias 127) 的"in-place exponent shifting"实现，**但缺少了 exponent rebias**：`(15-7)<<23` = `0x04000000` 的 fp32 magic number 加法或乘法常数。这正是用户怀疑的同形态 bug。

现在去找 mainloop 中调用点 + vLLM 上游对应实现。

227	// Wait until barrier reaches `count`, then lock for current threadblock.
228	__device__ inline void barrier_acquire(int* lock, int count) {
229	  if (threadIdx.x == 0) {
230	    int state = -1;
231	    do
232	      // Guarantee that subsequent writes by this threadblock will be visible
233	      // globally.
234	      asm volatile("ld.global.acquire.gpu.b32 %0, [%1];\n" : "=r"(state) : "l"(lock));
235	    while (state != count);
236	  }
237	  __syncthreads();
238	}
239	
240	// Release barrier and increment visitation count.
241	__device__ inline void barrier_release(int* lock, bool reset = false) {
242	  __syncthreads();
243	  if (threadIdx.x == 0) {
244	    if (reset) {
245	      lock[0] = 0;
246	      return;
247	    }
248	    int val = 1;
249	    // Make sure that all writes since acquiring this barrier are visible
250	    // globally, while releasing the barrier.
251	    asm volatile("fence.acq_rel.gpu;\n");
252	    asm volatile("red.relaxed.gpu.global.add.s32 [%0], %1;\n" : : "l"(lock), "r"(val));
253	  }
254	}

> DEVELOPER

背景：我在 RTX 6000D (sm_120, Blackwell consumer) 上做 GEMM 底层调优。ncu 被 SKU 锁，能用的工具是 cuobjdump SASS + nsys timeline + cudaFuncGetAttributes + ncu_occupancy Python API + Triton ttgir/ttpx dump。已经做完宏观调研（autotune tile sweep / schedule 选型 / CUTLASS 升级评估），现在要进 kernel 内部做寄存器、SMEM、pipeline 级别的底层手段调研。

我已知的事实（不要再调研宏观）：
- sm_120 max warps/SM=48, register file 64K×32-bit/SM, SMEM/block=99KB, max blocks/SM=32
- 当前 NVFP4 GEMM REG=168 → occupancy = floor(64K/(168×32))/48 = 12/48 = 25%
- Marlin REG 100-127 → occupancy 31-42%
- sm_120 走 mma.sync warp 级（不是 sm_100 tcgen05）；没有 TMEM 兜底
- 没有 ncu，但有 cuobjdump --dump-resource-usage + --dump-sass
- 没有 GPUscout / CUPTI Range Profiler / Zymtrace（Blackwell SKU 锁 + PCSampling 整族砍）

调研任务：用 web search / web fetch + 读 PTX ISA 9.x、CUDA C++ Programming Guide、SASS instruction reference、CUTLASS / Triton 源码，调研 **GPU GEMM kernel 在没有 ncu 情况下的真正底层调优手段**：

A. **register pressure 精确定位**：
1. 怎么从 cuobjdump SASS 输出推断哪些是真正持有 mma frag 的 reg vs 哪些是临时 spill candidate？
2. nvdisasm --print-life-ranges 的输出怎么解读？哪些 reg 跨 mainloop iter 活跃 vs 单 iter local？
3. STACK > 0（我们当前 STACK=0-16）是 spill 信号吗？还是仅 local var array?
4. 业界（CUTLASS / Triton 社区）用什么手段精确测某个 reg 是 spill 临界点（看 LDL/STL count? 看 cubin sectionheader?）？

B. **SMEM bank conflict 探测（无 ncu）**：
1. ncu 锁了，怎么从 SASS 静态推断 bank conflict？哪些 LDS/STS 模式 = 32 thread 跨 32 bank 一致？
2. 微基准方法（自写小 kernel + cudaEvent + 调 stride 看 cycle time 跳变）能不能定量探测 bank conflict？开源工具？
3. CUTLASS swizzle (`Swizzle<3,4,3>` 之类) 在 sub-byte (FP4 4-bit)、FP8、BF16 各自的 bank conflict-free 配置怎么算？业界有验证脚本吗？
4. cuobjdump SASS 里 LDSM (ldmatrix) 是单条还是多条 transaction？怎么从 SASS 看 ldmatrix 是 4×4 / 4×8 / 8×8 哪种 mode？

## Search Results Summary

I found relevant information about nvdisasm's register liveness analysis capabilities. Here are the key findings:

### Register Liveness Range Information

nvdisasm is capable of showing the register (general and predicate) liveness range information. For each line of CUDA assembly, nvdisasm displays whether a given device register was assigned, accessed, live or re-assigned. It also shows the total number of registers used.

### Life Range Mode Options

The `--life-range-mode` (-lrm) option implies option `--print-life-ranges`, and determines how register live range info should be printed with three allowed values: 'count' (not printing details, leaving only the # column of live registers), 'narrow' (a one-character column for each register, economizing on table width), and 'wide' (columns spaced out for readability, which is the default).

### CUDA SASS Analysis Context

nvdisasm extracts information from standalone cubin files and presents them in human readable format. The output of nvdisasm includes CUDA assembly code for each kernel, listing of ELF data sections and other CUDA specific sections. Output style and options are controlled through nvdisasm command-line options.

This tool is commonly used for analyzing NVIDIA GPU SASS (Streaming Multiprocessor Assembly) code, particularly for understanding register pressure and optimization opportunities in compiled CUDA binaries.

# NVFP4 BF16 Dequantization Bug Fix

Based on the PR discussion, the bug involved **incorrect exponent widening in the S0E5M3 to BF16 conversion** within the Marlin kernel's dequantization logic.

## The Problem

The original code assumed weight scales would always be large enough (MSB=1 after multiplying by 2^7) to safely convert to BF16. However, models with `global_scale=1` and certain MoE configurations produced scales so small they underflowed to zero when cast to FP16 (min normal ~6.1e-5), causing garbled output.

## The Solution

Rather than modifying the kernel, the fix implements **Python-side rescaling**:

**File:** `vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/utils/marlin_utils_fp4.py`

The PR added:
- `_nvfp4_compute_scale_factor()`: Calculates the minimum power-of-2 multiplier needed to lift scales into FP16's normal range
- Modified `nvfp4_marlin_process_scales()`: Applies rescaling before S0E5M3 conversion, returning both processed scales and the scale factor
- Updated all call sites: Divide `global_scale` by the scale factor to maintain mathematical equivalence

**Key principle:** "Rescale weight scales in Python by a power-of-2 factor so all non-zero values satisfy the MSB=1 assumption after `* 2^7`, then compensate by dividing `global_scale` accordingly."

This prevents underflow while maintaining zero runtime overhead when no rescaling is needed (K=1.0).

Based on the search results, here's information about CUTLASS swizzle, bank conflicts, and ldmatrix with FP4, FP8, and BF16 layouts:

## Swizzle and Bank Conflicts

Swizzling allows the ldmatrix.m8n8 instruction to load an 8x16B/16Bx8 subtile (within a larger tile) in 1 cycle without SMEM bank conflicts. During ldmatrix operations, every thread in a phase accesses the same bank simultaneously, creating 8-way bank conflicts, which is why swizzling is essential.

## Swizzle Layout Patterns

The swizzle layout should serve the 8x16B load pattern of ldmatrix.m8n8 at full SMEM read bandwidth (128B/cycle). The 8x16B subtile the ldmatrix.m8n8 instruction loads is exactly 1 swizzle none atom, and all chunks are stored contiguously in SMEM, allowing ldmatrix.m8n8 to load all chunks in 1 cycle without bank conflicts.

## FP8, BF16, and Low-Precision Support

The ldmatrix (stmatrix) instruction is designed to help warp threads collectively load (store) GEMM matrices from shared memory to registers (registers to shared memory). However, ldmatrix assumes each matrix element holds 16-bits of data. For FP8 (8-bits) operations, to work around this limitation, the instruction loads 16-bits and uses this to fill 2 FP8 values per load.

## SM100/SM120 (Blackwell) Considerations

Only 128B swizzling patterns, or no swizzling, is supported on newer architectures like Blackwell (SM100/SM120).

The search results provide technical details about swizzle implementations for bank conflict avoidance but don't contain specific sm_100 or sm_120 architecture details beyond the swizzling constraints mentioned.

## Key Findings:

**setmaxnreg Instruction**: setmaxnreg is a new feature since Hopper (SM 90 and later). This instruction allows for dynamic control of register allocation at the warp level, which can affect occupancy and enable warp specialization techniques.

**Warp Specialization and Register Reallocation**: DeepSeek has demonstrated partitioning Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs) into specialized warp-level communication tasks with customized PTX instructions, employing warp specialization technique. This relates to using setmaxnreg for different warps to have different register allocations within the same kernel.

**SM Architecture Support**: Each kernel is executed as a batch of threads organized as a grid of clusters consisting of CTAs where cluster is optional level and is applicable only for target architectures sm_90 and higher. This indicates that sm_90, sm_100, and sm_120 (Hopper, Blackwell initial, and newer Blackwell) all support the advanced features related to warp-level control.

The NVIDIA PTX ISA 8.7 documentation (released February 27, 2025) contains the latest specification for setmaxnreg and related instructions for these GPU architectures, though the search results show only the table of contents reference to the instruction rather than its full documentation details.

# PR #37502 Summary: Marlin NVFp4 Rescaling Fix

## Changed File
**`vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/utils/marlin_utils_fp4.py`**

## Key Changes

The PR modifies the `_nvfp4_compute_scale_factor` function (lines 31-40) to address rescaling issues:

**Previous logic:** Ensured all rescaled values were `>= 2` by focusing on minimum values.

**New logic:** The function now normalizes scales based on maximum values to better utilize FP8 E4M3's dynamic range. Specifically, it:
- Clamps scales that are too small to zero
- Computes scale factors so maximum values approach ~448.0 (FP8 E4M3 maximum)
- Returns power-of-2 scale factors `>= 1.0`

## Critical Detail for Your Investigation

The docstring wasn't updated to reflect the substantive logic changes, which a reviewer flagged as potentially misleading. The new implementation prioritizes maximum value normalization rather than minimum value thresholds—this shift in rescaling strategy may interact with your FP8→BF16 widening concerns.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about your query:

## Key Findings

The RTX 5090 is based on the Blackwell architecture (sm_120) and features new TMA (Tensor Memory Accelerator) hardware introduced in Hopper and refined in Blackwell.

### cp.async.bulk.tensor.tile and TMA

Instead of 256 threads each loading one element, a single thread issues one cp.async.bulk.tensor.2d command that describes the entire 2D tile — "load a 32×224 block of floats starting at row R, column C." The TMA hardware unit, separate from the CUDA cores, handles the entire transfer via DMA.

### RTX 5090 (Consumer Blackwell) Architecture

The RTX 5090 is a consumer-grade Blackwell GPU with sm_120 architecture. However, there's an important architectural distinction: SM120 uses the older HMMA instruction family (the same register-to-register MMA approach used since Volta/Ampere) and the TMEM hardware is physically absent from the GB202 die. 

The "Blackwell" branding shared between the RTX 5090 and B200/B300 obscures what are functionally different GPU architectures for compute workloads. SM120's tensor cores are powerful but architecturally closer to Hopper than to data center Blackwell.

Blackwell's TMA unit shares the same PTX interface as Hopper's; the practical difference observed is that Blackwell favors larger per-thread tiles (TM=28 is optimal on the 5090 vs TM=8 on the H200).

Based on the search results, here's what I found regarding your query about `mma.sync mxf4nvf4 block_scale scale_vec PTX 9 register layout scale factor`:

The `mma.sync.aligned.m16n8k64.row.col .kind::mxf4nvf4.block_scale.scale_vec::4X .f32.e2m1.e2m1.f32.ue4m3` instruction is a PTX tensor core instruction supported on SM120+ architectures.

Regarding register and scale factor layout:

The `.scale_vec::4X` format is only available for the mxf4nvf4 data type, and the scale factor vector is Mx4 per MMA block.

For block-scaled MMA instructions with mxf4nvf4, the PTX inline assembly includes scale factor A and B registers along with Block/Thread ID parameters in the instruction format.

For more detailed information about register layouts and scale factor organization, the PTX 9 documentation includes sections on the packing format used for matrices A and B by `.kind::mxf4nvf4` in shared memory, as well as the layout of scale factor matrices for different block sizes.

The official NVIDIA PTX ISA 9.2 documentation would contain comprehensive details about the exact register layout specifications and scale factor positioning for these instructions.

## Register Pressure and Spill Detection in Triton

The `USE_IR_LOC={ttir,ttgir}` environment variable reparses the IR such that the location information will be the line number of the IR file with that particular extension, instead of line number of the python file, which can provide a direct mapping from the IR to llir/ptx.

If you find inefficiencies, you can trace it back to LLVM IR, TTGIR and even TTIR to see where the problem comes from.

### Register Spill Information

The search results show that Triton reports register spills information that is leveraged by torch inductor to skip suboptimal tuning configs. 

### Register Pressure Optimization

Loop strength reduction is known to cause up to 10% performance changes for certain kernels with register pressure. This can be controlled with the `DISABLE_LLVM_OPT` flag.

However, the search results don't contain specific information about a "register pressure spill detection workflow without ncu" for Triton. The results mention TTGIR and TTIR IR representations but don't detail a specific workflow by that name. Based on the search results, here's what I found regarding RTX 5090 sm_120 GEMM tuning and profiling challenges:

## Key Issues Found

CUTLASS 3.8 only supports up to sm_100a, and users with RTX 5090 want to try GEMM kernels using new MMA instructions introduced in sm_120.

### GEMM Kernel Issues on SM120

NVFP4 mm_fp4 GEMM backends have failed on RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs, with cutlass producing zeros and cudnn failing with unsupported graph errors. All native FP4 MoE backends produce garbage output or crash on SM120 due to broken CUTLASS grouped GEMM templates, though patching FlashInfer 0.6.5 achieved correct native FP4 MoE output albeit at reduced speed (14.6 tok/s vs 46-49 tok/s).

### Dispatcher and Optimization Issues

While profiling FP32 SGEMM on RTX 5090, cublasSgemmStridedBatched dispatches the same cutlass_80_simt_sgemm_128x32_8x5 kernel for every batched workload from 256×256 to 8192×8192×8 at ~40% FMA pipe utilization, and the dispatcher does not escalate to larger tiles at any threshold.

### Compiler Flag Issues

The compute_120 flag (without "a") doesn't define __CUDA_ARCH_FEAT_SM120_ALL, causing CUTLASS_GDC_ENABLED guard to evaluate to false, which can be addressed by adding the flag directly as a compiler flag.

The search results don't specifically address Nsight Compute profiler availability issues or dedicated workarounds, but they document significant compatibility and optimization challenges with SM120 GEMM operations.

# FP4 Marlin Scale Processing Analysis

## `_nvfp4_compute_scale_factor`

This function computes a power-of-2 rescaling factor to ensure all non-zero scale values satisfy a specific invariant after transformation.

**Key Logic:**
- Multiplies marlin_scales by 2^7: `ws_float = marlin_scales.float() * (2**7)`
- Computes maximum value among non-zero elements
- If `max_val < 448 * (2**7)`, calculates: `sf = (448 * (2**7) / max_val).log2().floor().exp2()`
- Returns 1.0 for fp16 inputs (smaller dynamic range)

**Purpose:** Rescales weights so that after multiplying by 2^7, the MSB remains set to 1 for all non-zero scales.

## `nvfp4_marlin_process_scales`

This function transforms weight scales into S0E5M3 format for kernel consumption.

**Processing Steps:**

1. **Convert to half:** `marlin_scales = marlin_scales.to(torch.half)`

2. **Reorder layout:** `marlin_scales.view(-1, 4)[:, [0, 2, 1, 3]].view(marlin_scales.size(0), -1)`

3. **Apply scale factor:** If provided, multiply by it

4. **Multiply by 2^7 and clamp:** 
   - `marlin_scales = marlin_scales * (2**7)`
   - `marlin_scales[marlin_scales < 2] = 0`

5. **Bit-pack as int16 then reinterpret as fp8:**
   - `marlin_scales = marlin_scales.view(torch.int16) << 1`
   - `marlin_scales = marlin_scales.view(torch.float8_e4m3fn)`

6. **Extract every other element:** `marlin_scales[:, 1::2].contiguous()`

The S0E5M3 format exploits the MSB=1 invariant to achieve tighter exponent bias representation for dequantization speedup.
```

## PTX 9 Support for bf16x2 and e4m3x2

PTX 9 adds support for .bf16x2 destination type for cvt instruction with .e4m3x2, .e5m2x2, .e3m2x2, .e2m3x2, .e2m1x2 source types. This directly addresses your query about `cvt.rn.bf16x2.e4m3x2` support.

## Blackwell SM_120 Support for FP8/E4M3

The Blackwell SM120 GEMMs can be built using the collective builder interface, with examples in examples/79_blackwell_geforce_gemm/ and unit tests listed. The data types supported and tensor alignment requirements are the same as the Blackwell SM100 GEMMs.

For FP8 specifically, SM120's non-block-scaled FP8 MMA (m16n8k32 kind::f8f6f4) offers 2x theoretical throughput over BF16 (m16n8k16) for attention kernels.

## General PTX and Data Format Context

The e4m3 encoding is an 8-bit floating point format with 4 bits for exponent and 3 bits for mantissa. The e4m3 encoding does not support infinity and NaN values are limited to 0x7f and 0xff.

The search results confirm that Blackwell (including SM_120) has comprehensive support for these narrow precision data formats through the updated PTX ISA.

# Register Liveness and Analysis Flags

Based on the documentation, here are the relevant flags for register and resource analysis:

## nvdisasm Flags

**Register Liveness Analysis:**
- `--print-life-ranges` / `-plr`: "Print register life range information in a trailing column in the produced disassembly."
- `--life-range-mode` / `-lrm`: Controls display format with options `count`, `narrow`, or `wide` for register live range visualization.

The output shows register assignment (`^`), usage (`v`), reassignment (`x`), and in-use (`:`) states with a register count column.

## cuobjdump Flags

**Resource Usage:**
- `--dump-resource-usage` / `-res-usage`: "Dump resource usage for each ELF. Useful in getting all the resource usage information at one place."

Output format displays:
- Common resources: `GLOBAL`, `CONSTANT[n]`
- Per-function metrics: `REG` (register count), `STACK` (bytes), `SHARED`, `LOCAL`, `CONSTANT[n]`, `TEXTURE`, `SURFACE`, `SAMPLER`

## Important Note

The documentation does not reference flags for `--print-instruction-statistics`, `FRAME`, `SPILL STORES`, or `SPILL LOADS`. These specific fields are not mentioned in the provided content, so they may exist in other CUDA tools or newer versions not covered here.

# Analysis of cuobjdump --dump-resource-usage Output

Based on the NVIDIA Developer Forum discussion provided, here's what the documentation clarifies:

## STACK Definition

According to Robert Crovella (NVIDIA expert): **"Stack usage is also typically not evident/fully explicit at the C++ level... Zero stack usage might be reasonable for code that is fully inlined."**

The expert explains that stack usage relates to call frames and is largely a compiler artifact rather than something explicitly controlled by developers.

## Important Clarification on Stack vs. Spill

The forum discussion does **not** contain information about "FRAME," "SPILL STORES," or "SPILL LOADS" in the cuobjdump output. These specific metrics are not explained in the provided content.

However, regarding stack and spilling generally, the expert notes: **"[Local memory] may also include local usage associated with register 'spilling', i.e. values that are sometimes in registers but sometimes not, and need a backing store."**

## Stack Overflow Risk

The discussion emphasizes a critical hazard: when functions are called (particularly with recursion), excessive stack usage can cause out-of-bounds memory access—which matches your reported issue where inlined functions work but called functions fail.

## Recommendation

For CUDA Fortran specifics about spill metrics and stack management, the expert suggests consulting the **nvfortran compiler forum**, as the provided discussion focuses primarily on CUDA C++.

Based on the search results, I found comprehensive information about CUTLASS SM120 FP4/NVFP4 support and related components. Here's what the search revealed:

## SM120 NVFP4 CUTLASS Support

NVFP4 SM120 kernels are compiled and available in vLLM 0.13.0 with dedicated files for scaled matrix multiplication and blockwise MoE kernels.

## Known Issues

CUTLASS grouped GEMM templates produce garbage output on SM120 desktop Blackwell GPUs, and the CUTLASS TMA Warp Specialized grouped GEMM kernels fail at runtime with all 80 fast tactics producing initialization errors.

## Dequantization and Data Layout

When CUTLASS kernels fail, the system falls back to Marlin, which dequantizes FP4 weights to FP16 and runs standard GEMM. Scale Factor tensors have an interleaved layout in CUTLASS NVFP4 GEMM implementations.

## FP4 to BF16 Conversion

The output dtype for FP4 GEMM operations can be bf16 or fp16, with bf16 supported across backends.

The search results indicate these are ongoing compatibility issues with SM120 (Blackwell) architecture, particularly with the TMA Warp Specialized kernels that are critical for NVFP4 performance.

Based on the search results, I found information about FP8 to BF16 conversions in CUDA environments. Here's what I discovered:

## FP8 to BF16 Conversion Support

The `cvt.rn.bf16x2.e4m3x2` instruction is part of FP8 conversion instructions needed by llm.c, and involves extending the PTX parser to recognize new fp8 conversion instructions with e4m3x2 and e5m2x2 types.

## Data Type Specifications

The e4m3 data format is an 8-bit floating point format with 4 bits for exponent and 3 bits for mantissa. A register variable containing bf16 data must be declared with .b16 type.

## Packed Format Implementation

For an instruction with instruction type as .bf16x2, all of the operand variables must be of type .b32. This means the `cvt.rn.bf16x2.e4m3x2` instruction operates on 32-bit registers containing two packed bf16 values.

The search results reference implementation details from NVIDIA's PTX documentation and the ZLUDA project, which provide the foundational support for these specialized floating-point conversion instructions that are optimized for newer GPU architectures like SM_100 and SM_120.

# Fragment Layout Analysis: mma.sync.m16n8k64 FP4 E2M1 Block Scale on SM120

Based on the forum post provided, I must note that **the exact fragment layout documentation for this specific instruction is not available in the source material**.

## What the Post Reveals

The original question explicitly states the documentation gap: the author searched for "the fragment layout diagram specifically for FP4 E2M1 with block scaling" but could not find it. They note that "the PTX ISA 9.2 documentation provides fragment layout tables for m16n8k32 with types like .f16, .bf16, .u8, .s8 (Tables 43-47), and the m16n8k64 section mentions the instruction exists, but I could not find the fragment layout diagram."

## Known Parameters (from the instruction)

The instruction structure is:
```
mma.sync.aligned.m16n8k64.row.col.kind::mxf8f6f4.block_scale.scale_vec::2X.f32.e2m1.e2m1.f32
```

The author specifies:
- Matrix A: 16×64, FP4 E2M1, 4 × 32-bit registers per thread (a0-a3), 8 FP4 values per register
- Matrix D (accumulator): 16×8 FP32, 4 FP32 registers per thread

## Conclusion

**The exact register-to-thread mapping for this configuration is not documented in the provided content.** The post itself is a request for this missing information, referencing external resources (CUTLASS issues, third-party kernels) that aren't included in the excerpt.

# FP4 Sub-byte GEMM on Blackwell: Limitations in Available Documentation

Based on the provided content, I must note significant gaps in coverage of your specific technical questions.

## What the Article Addresses

The tutorial covers FP4 (E2M1) as one of five supported sub-byte formats, explaining that data in SMEM must follow "a particular 16-byte aligned format" where "16 consecutive 4-bit or 6-bit elements are packed contiguously and then padded to 16-byte boundaries."

For TMA operations, the document mentions `CU_TENSOR_MAP_DATA_TYPE_16U4_ALIGN16B` (`.b4x16_p64`) for loading packed 4-bit data with padding requirements including "32B aligned" base addresses and leading dimensions that are "a multiple of 128 elements."

## Critical Gaps

The article **does not provide**:
- Specific swizzle mode support details for sm_100 or sm_120
- Information about `ldmatrix` behavior with FP4
- Bank conflict avoidance strategies for sub-byte formats
- PTX or SASS instruction names beyond generic references to `tcgen05.mma`
- Comparisons between sm_100 TMEM-based and sm_120 warp-level implementations

The document explicitly defers detailed discussion: "We defer a discussion of block-scaling to the next post" (which apparently remains unpublished as of January 2026).

**For authoritative technical specifications**, consult NVIDIA's [PTX documentation](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/parallel-thread-execution/) and CUTLASS source code directly.

Based on the provided code, there is **no PTX cvt instruction for direct FP8 (e4m3) or FP4 (e2m1) to BF16 conversion**.

The file shows FP8 casting operations, but they use indirect conversion paths:

```cpp
template<> __device__ inline __nv_bfloat162 
cuda_cast<__nv_bfloat162, __nv_fp8x2_e4m3>(__nv_fp8x2_e4m3 val) { 
  return fp8x2_e4m3_to_bfloat2(&val); 
}
```

This converts through a helper function `fp8x2_e4m3_to_bfloat2()` rather than using PTX assembly. There are no inline asm strings with `cvt` instructions for FP8/FP4 to BF16 conversions visible in this file.

The only inline asm `cvt` instructions present handle FP16/FP32 to int8 conversions (lines converting half and float to signed 8-bit integers), not FP8-to-BF16 conversions.

Based on the search results, I found relevant information about the `cvt.rn.bf16x2.e2m1x2` CUDA inline assembly instruction you're asking about.

## Key Findings

The `cvt.rn.bf16x2` instruction adds support for .bf16x2 destination type for cvt instruction with .e2m1x2 source types, which is exactly the conversion pattern you're interested in (converting from FP4 E2M1 packed format to BF16 packed format).

### Technical Details

The E2M1 data format is a 4-bit floating point format with 2 bits for exponent and 1 bit for mantissa. The e2m1 encoding does not support infinity and NaN. e2m1 values must be used in a packed format specified as e2m1x2.

A register variable containing two e2m1 values must be declared with .b8 type.

For the output: All of the operand variables must be of type .b32 for an instruction with instruction type as .bf16x2.

### Support Status

The `cvt.rn.satfinite.e2m1x2.f32` PTX instruction for FP32->FP4 conversion is available on SM120 family but only when compiled for sm120f (family-conditional instructions).

This information indicates that the conversion instructions you're looking for are part of PTX 9.2 specifications and are supported on Blackwell architecture (SM120), but the exact inline assembly example code wasn't found in the search results. You would need to reference the official NVIDIA PTX ISA documentation directly for complete code examples.

# Marlin CUDA Kernel Analysis

## Dequant Function
Located at **lines 314-339**, the `dequant` function converts a single int32 quantized value into a `FragB` (4 fp16 values):

> "Efficiently dequantize an int32 value into a full B-fragment of 4 fp16 values."

The function uses inline PTX with `lop3` operations for bitwise manipulation.

## Main Loop Interleaving

The **`matmul` lambda (lines 651-673)** handles the interleaving. Per iteration, there are **4 MMA calls per dequant call**:

> "for (int j = 0; j < 4; j++) { int b_quant = frag_b_quant[k % 2][j]; FragB frag_b0 = dequant(b_quant);"

This loop dequantizes one int32 per iteration (j=0 to 3), producing 2 FragB values via `dequant()`, then executes **2 MMA operations per dequant** for each of the `thread_m_blocks`. Total: approximately **2 MMA calls per dequant call**.

## PTX Inline Assembly for Conversion

The `dequant` function uses **`lop3.b32`** (lines 327-335) for bitwise operations, and the output converts to `half2` via pointer casting rather than explicit `cvt` instructions. The `__hsub2` and `__hfma2` intrinsics (lines 347-352) handle fp16 arithmetic without dedicated inline CVT assembly.

**No dedicated `cvt` or scale conversion PTX inline assembly** is present; conversions rely on CUDA intrinsics.

Based on the search results, I found relevant information about the topics in your query. Here's what I found:

## vLLM Marlin/GPTQ-Marlin and FP4 Support

NVFP4 quantized models produce garbled output when running with --dtype bfloat16 on GPUs without native FP4 support (e.g., RTX 4090 SM89, V100 SM70), as these GPUs fall back to the Marlin kernel for FP4 weight dequantization.

### FE2M1 and Exponent Widening Issue

The dequant_fp8_scales function in csrc/quantization/marlin/dequant.h has incorrect exponent widening from S0E5M3 (5-bit exponent, bias 15) to BF16 (8-bit exponent, bias 127), producing BF16 exponent with 3 middle exponent bits always zero instead of the correct pattern. This creates a gap in the exponent space — for most real model scale values, the BF16 scale is interpreted as ~2^(-112) instead of ~2^0, causing weight × scale to underflow to zero.

### SM120 Support Limitations

The MXFP4 backend selection in vllm only checks for SM100 family, while SM120 doesn't match this check, and the Triton backend check similarly excludes SM120. SM121 (Blackwell) does not have native hardware FP4 support, so weight-only FP4 compression uses the Marlin kernel.

### Marlin Kernel Optimizations

Marlin fuses dequantization with computation: it loads 4-bit weight asynchronously while bypassing L1, then dequantizes and computes in the same fused kernel, eliminating extra memory round-trips, kernel launch overhead, and intermediate storage.

# Using nvdisasm/cuobjdump to Inspect SASS Control Codes

## Basic Usage

The tool processes output from `cuobjdump` or `nvdisasm` with specific flags. According to the script, you can run:

```
nvdisasm -hex program.cubin | ./nvdisasm_overlay.py
```

Or supply a disassembly file directly to the Python script.

## Output Format

The script augments disassembly with control code information in this structure:

**`[ FIXED LATENCY | VARIABLE LATENCY | OTHER ]`**

Breaking this down:
- **FIXED LATENCY**: Stall cycle count (0-15) and yield indicator ('Y' or blank)
- **VARIABLE LATENCY**: Write barrier (WR1-8), read barrier (RD1-8), and barrier consumption as 6-bit mask
- **OTHER**: Optional batch markers (START, S_TILE, END, EXEMPT) and pipeline markers (PM values)

Example: `[ 5 Y | WR2 RD1 000011 ]` indicates 5 stall cycles with yield enabled, write barrier 2, read barrier 1, and two active barriers.

## Finding Spill Instructions

To locate memory spill operations (`LDL`/`STL`), use grep on the disassembly output:

```bash
nvdisasm -hex program.cubin | grep -E '\bLDL\b|\bSTL\b'
```

This identifies local load/store instructions that indicate register spilling, which are critical performance concerns in GPU kernels.
```

## Key Findings:

**Alignment Requirements for cp.async.bulk:**
Both srcMem and dstMem must be 16-byte aligned, and size must be a multiple of 16.

**Shared Memory Alignment (for TMA operations):**
When using TMA, the shared memory is required to be aligned to 128 bytes. Additionally, the tables define the mapping of the 16-byte chunks along the 128 bytes to eight subgroups of four banks.

**cp.async.bulk vs cp.async.cg:**
The search results show that these are fundamentally different instruction families:
- cp.async.bulk is Hopper's hardware-accelerated asynchronous bulk transfer family, uses TMA, and one thread can launch a whole tile transfer while the hardware tracks progress and updates the relevant completion object.
- cp.async.cg.shared.global is used to asynchronously copy data from global memory to shared memory, though it is available on earlier architectures like Ampere.

However, the search results don't contain specific comparisons of throughput between `cp.async.bulk` and `cp.async.cg`, or specific details about SM_120 behavior with these alignment constraints. For more detailed performance comparisons and SM_120-specific information, you may need to consult NVIDIA's PTX ISA documentation or architecture-specific programming guides.

Based on the search results, here's information relevant to your query about CUTLASS SM120 sub-byte GEMM kernels with warp-level mma.sync:

## Key Findings:

**SM120 and tcgen05.mma Architecture:**
SM120 does not support tcgen05.mma, so the FP4 path goes through warp-level mma.sync. This is a critical distinction for SM120 Blackwell GeForce RTX 50 series GPUs.

**Sub-Byte GEMM Support:**
CUTLASS 4.0 has added support for newly introduced narrow precision GEMMs, and similar to Blackwell SM100 GEMMs, the SM120 GEMMs can be built using the collective builder interface. Valid tile shapes are provided for {float8_t, float_6_t, float_4_t} x {float8_t, float_6_t, float_4_t} of SM120 GEMMs.

**SM120 Kernel Schedules:**
SM120 GEMMs support both pingpong and cooperative kernel schedules, where the pingpong kernel schedule has two groups of 4 MMA warps working on different output tiles, and the cooperative kernel schedule has only one group of 8 MMA warps working on the same output tile.

**References and Examples:**
Examples are available in examples/79_blackwell_geforce_gemm/, which would contain practical reference implementations for SM120 sub-byte GEMMs using warp-level mma.sync instructions.

**Architectural Limitations:**
The NVIDIA Blackwell SM100 architecture used in datacenter products has a different compute capability than SM120 underpinning NVIDIA Blackwell GeForce RTX 50 series GPUs, and kernels compiled for SM100 architecture are not compatible with RTX 50 series GPUs.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about `cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor` and the factors that limit occupancy:

## Function Purpose

`cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor` is an API that produces an occupancy prediction based on the block size and shared memory usage of your kernel, available since CUDA 6.5.

## Limiting Factors

The occupancy of a kernel is constrained by three main factors:

1. **Register Limitation**: If register usage is the limiting factor, it means the number of registers per thread allocated by the compiler can be reduced to increase occupancy.

2. **Shared Memory Limitation**: The SM has a fixed amount of shared memory shared by all active threads. If this factor is limiting active blocks, it means the shared memory needed per thread can be reduced to increase occupancy.

3. **Warp Limit**: The maximum number of concurrent warps per SM is 48 (for Ada architecture), and this is one of the factors influencing warp occupancy.

## How the Function Works

The function returns occupancy for a device function by taking parameters for the block size and dynamic shared memory size. The function can be used to calculate occupancy with shared memory by passing the dynamic shared memory size as a parameter.

# Bug Analysis: NVFP4 BF16 Exponent Widening Issue

Based on the GitHub issue, here's the core problem:

## The Bug

The `dequant_fp8_scales<nv_bfloat162, kFE4M3fn>` function in `csrc/quantization/marlin/dequant.h` incorrectly widens the exponent from S0E5M3 format (5-bit exponent with bias 15) to BF16 format (8-bit exponent with bias 127).

## What Goes Wrong

The implementation produces BF16 exponent `E4 0 0 0 E3 E2 E1 E0` instead of the correct `E4 !E4 !E4 !E4 E3 E2 E1 E0`. This creates a critical exponent space gap: "for most real model scale values (E4=0), the BF16 scale is interpreted as ~2^(-112) instead of ~2^0, causing weight × scale to underflow to zero."

## Impact

This affects all BF16 NVFP4 quantized models on GPUs without native FP4 support (SM < 100, including RTX 4090). The issue manifests as "54.7% of output values are zero" and "cos_sim = 0.22 vs FP32 reference (essentially random)."

## Resolution

The issue links to PR #34577 as the fix, though the exact code modifications aren't included in the provided content. The solution involves correcting the exponent rebias operation during the S0E5M3-to-BF16 conversion.
```

# W4A8 Marlin PR Summary

Based on the PR description, this implementation adds W4A8 support to the Marlin kernel with the following key changes:

## What Was Added

The PR introduces a **new MMA (matrix multiply-accumulate) execution path** optimized for INT8/FP8 activations, rather than modifying the existing dequantization sequence. The implementation includes:

1. **New Weight Layout**: A redesigned weight layout to accommodate "m16n8k32 mma instructions for INT8/FP8 and enable a single warp to process weights within the same group"

2. **Scale Path Modifications**: For W4A8-INT8 specifically, scales were quantized to INT32 to reduce "overhead of these type conversions" when multiplying INT32 accumulators by scales

3. **Dequantization Support**: The PR adds dequantization logic for converting INT4 weights (both GPTQ and AWQ formats) to INT8, and INT4 to FP8 with special preprocessing

## Architecture Changes

Rather than altering `dequant.h` internals, the implementation introduces:
- Separate kernel code paths for W4A8 vs. W4A16
- Preprocessing of weights during loading for FP8 compatibility
- L2 cache optimization using "DP + one-tile SK and DP + two-tile SK" scheduling

The approach preserves existing dequantization infrastructure while adding specialized computation units for lower-precision activation types.

# setmaxnreg and SM90 Occupancy

## Does setmaxnreg dynamically change occupancy?

**No.** According to Greg's response: "The total number of registers allocated to all warps in the CTA cannot exceed the initial CTA launch. Due to this constraint SM warp occupancy is not changed."

## Warpgroup Register Quota Model

The `setmaxnreg` instruction allows dynamic register redistribution within a thread block:

- Producer warps can return registers via `setmaxnreg.dec`
- Consumer warps can acquire registers via `setmaxnreg.inc`
- The total CTA register pool remains constant

## Static vs. Dynamic Measurement

Occupancy calculation uses the **static launch-time register count**, not dynamic changes. As noted: "NCU captures the number of registers per warp at grid launch...NCU does not have a method to trace the changes."

However, the occupancy metric itself **remains valid and useful** because the total register constraint never changes—only the distribution among warps varies at runtime. The observed NCU value (168 registers) represents an effective average across the variable runtime allocations within the fixed CTA-level budget.
```

# SM120 NVFP4 MoE Bug Fix Summary

## The Core Problem
CUTLASS grouped block-scaled FP4 GEMM kernels produce "garbage output" on SM120 desktop Blackwell GPUs, generating incoherent token sequences like random whitespace and fragments instead of coherent text.

## Working FlashInfer Patches
The fix required modifications to 10+ files across FlashInfer and vLLM:

**Key changes:**
- Modified capability checks from SM100-only to include SM120 across three vLLM files
- Added major version 12 support to FlashInfer's JIT architecture filters
- Expanded CuTe DSL `admissible_archs` lists to include `"sm_120a"` in 18+ locations across five files
- Updated device mapping to recognize SM120 as `"Blackwell"` with `"sm_120a"` architecture
- Changed hardcoded equality checks to greater-than-or-equal in TRT-LLM launcher

## The compute_120f Breakthrough
The `compute_120f` flag (available only with CUDA 13.0+) unlocks "the fast TMA WS grouped GEMM tactics that failed with `compute_120a`." This architecture designation provides the complete SM120 feature set, enabling previously failing kernel initialization.

## Kernel Schedule Behavior
- **Cooperative schedule**: Works but slow on SM120
- **Pingpong schedule** (`KernelPtrArrayTmaWarpSpecializedPingpong`): Causes segmentation fault on SM120
- TMA warp-specialized tactics: Fail initialization with `compute_120a`, succeed with `compute_120f`

## Performance Metrics
| Configuration | Speed | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Marlin W4A16 | 46-49 tok/s | Correct |
| FlashInfer + compute_120f | 39.0 tok/s | Correct |
| FlashInfer + compute_120a | 14.6-14.9 tok/s | Correct but slow |

The ~20% gap between native FP4 and Marlin stems from activation quantization overhead and autotuner suboptimality.

## Nsight Compute Mention
No reference to Nsight Compute appears in this documentation.

# SM120 vs SM100: Key Differences

## Instructions Available on SM120

SM120 uses **warp-level `mma.sync.aligned` instructions** rather than SM100's warp-group `tcgen05.mma` instructions. Available variants include:

- `mma.sync.aligned.kind::f8f6f4` (mixed precision)
- `mma.sync.aligned.kind::mxf8f6f4.block_scale` (block-scaled mixed precision)
- `mma.sync.aligned.kind::mxf4.block_scale` (block-scaled 4-bit)
- `mma.sync.aligned.kind::mxf4nvf4.block_scale` (block-scaled variants)

## Features NOT Available on SM120

- **tcgen05 instructions** (SM100-specific warp-group operations)
- **TMA (Tensor Memory Accelerator)** support
- **Multicast capability** for cluster launches

## Kernel Schedule Models

SM120 supports two distinct pipeline approaches:

**Pingpong Schedule**: "two groups of 4 MMA warps working on different output tiles, overlapping the mainloop and epilogue"

**Cooperative Schedule**: "only one group of 8 MMA warps working on the same output tile"

When `KernelScheduleAuto` is selected, the cooperative approach becomes the default.

## Tile Shape Constraints

SM120 tile configurations are more restrictive than SM100. For float_6_t outputs, "the tile size in the leading dimension of output tensor must be 128." Supported MMA shapes include 64x64x128, 64x128x128, 128x64x128, and 128x128x128.

## Example Locations

- Non-block-scaled examples: `examples/79_blackwell_geforce_gemm/`
- Unit tests: `test/unit/gemm/device/sm120_tensorop_gemm/` and `sm120_blockscaled_tensorop_gemm/`

I found several relevant results about CUTLASS, Blackwell GPUs, and sub-byte GEMM operations. Here's what the search revealed:

## Key Findings

The CUTLASS TMA will use the special 16 byte aligned TMA for fp4 and fp6 based on the unpacksmem data types. Only 128B swizzling patterns, or no swizzling, is supported.

### SW128 Layout and Swizzling

Layout_K_SW128_Atom is a 128 byte wide swizzle for K-major A of data TypeA. The width of the swizzle is determined by the size of the tile in the contiguous dimension. In this case, the K dimension has 4 tiles of size 16 and half-precision is 2 bytes, so the width is 16*4*2=128 bytes.

### FP4 Data Handling

For FP4 operations specifically, operand data in SMEM must be stored in a particular 16-byte aligned format, where 16 consecutive 4-bit or 6-bit elements are packed contiguously and then padded to 16-byte boundaries.

### ldmatrix and UMMA

tcgen05.mma operates directly on shared memory (no need to load them to registers as ldmatrix does).

The search results primarily come from Colfax Research tutorials on CUTLASS and NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, which appear to be comprehensive technical resources on this topic.

## Key Results:

**Shared Memory Bank Architecture:**
Shared memory is organized into 32 banks, where each bank is a slice of SRAM that can load or store 4 bytes of data every cycle.

**Microbenchmarking Approaches:**
The search results include discussions of microbenchmarking techniques for measuring shared memory performance. PTX instructions can be marked as volatile, which is a directive for the PTX assembler that prevents optimization of loads. This technique is used in microbenchmarks to ensure memory operations aren't optimized away.

**Bank Conflict Profiling:**
NVIDIA Compute Profiler (nvprof) or NVIDIA Nsight tools can be used to identify bank conflicts in CUDA applications, providing metrics specifically related to shared memory bank conflicts.

**PTX and Optimization:**
Inline PTX can be used to enforce 128-bit shared memory operations to avoid bank conflicts.

The search results contain academic papers and technical discussions about measuring CUDA performance characteristics, particularly around how shared memory bank conflicts impact kernel execution cycles and methods to detect and mitigate them using profiling tools like Nsight Compute.

Based on the search results, here's information about the ldmatrix PTX instruction with 8x8 m8n8 modes:

## Register Count by Mode

For ldmatrix.x4 loading four 8x8 matrices, 4 output registers are required. More specifically:

- ldmatrix.sync.aligned.m8n8.x1 requires 1 register, .x2 requires 2 registers, and .x4 requires 4 registers

## Bytes Per Thread and Data Layout

When reading an 8x8 matrix, a contiguous set of four threads loads 16 bytes. Each element is 16 bits (half precision), so an 8x8 tile contains 64 elements or 128 bytes.

## Transpose and Non-Transpose Modes

The ldmatrix instruction is usually used for loading matrix fragments from shared memory to registers for MMA operations. CuTe provides wrappers including SM75_U32x1_LDSM_N, SM75_U32x2_LDSM_N, SM75_U32x4_LDSM_N for non-transposed loads and SM75_U16x2_LDSM_T, SM75_U16x4_LDSM_T, SM75_U16x8_LDSM_T for transposed loads.

The instruction syntax is: .shape = {.m8n8, .m16n16}; .num = {.x1, .x2, .x4}; .ss = {.shared{::cta}}; .type = {.b16, .b8}

# Summary: Swizzle<3,4,3> Bank Conflict Patterns

Based on the forum discussion, the technical answer is nuanced:

**For which element widths it works:**
The Swizzle<3,4,3> pattern (SW128 mode) is designed as a "bank conflict optimisation on the write side" for tensor operations. It effectively handles elements of 128 bits or larger. Per the NVIDIA documentation cited, when smaller elements are used, the shape must be adjusted: "For smaller element sizes, the same shapes would get multiplied along the leading dimension by a factor of `128 / sizeof_bits(Element)`."

**Key insight about the repetition:**
The swizzle element size is 16 bytes, meaning "each element (a vector of 8 values in the case of BF16) spans four smem banks and is 16B aligned. The 128B swizzling mode pattern actually repeats after 1024B."

**For sub-byte data (4-bit):**
The forum discussion doesn't explicitly address 4-bit data conflicts. However, the scaling rule implies that 4-bit elements would require substantial shape expansion (32x multiplication factor), potentially creating situations where the fixed 128-byte swizzle cycle cannot maintain conflict-free access patterns across all rows—particularly if memory access patterns don't align with the expanded tiling requirements.

The swizzle optimizes write-side patterns specifically for WGMMA/tcgen05 hardware instructions rather than general read patterns.

## Key Findings:

The PTX primitive `setmaxnreg` adjusts the registers allocated to the threads in the warpgroup. This is used in CUTLASS kernels for register optimization.

Producer warps (which only load data) typically need fewer registers than consumer warps (which do math), especially when using TMA. In the context of your query with producer count 40 and consumer count 232, this reflects the typical pattern where consumer threads require significantly more registers.

In the Hopper architecture, one thread can own up to 255 registers, and setmaxnreg can be set to a value between 24 and 256 (inclusive) at multiples of 8.

SM120 has an FP8 MMA instruction with PTX: mma.sync.aligned.kind::f8f6f4.m16n8k32.row.col.f32.e4m3.e4m3.f32, which relates to the synchronized, aligned instruction type in your query.

The specific register counts (producer 40, consumer 232) appear to be optimization parameters for a warp-specialized cooperative kernel targeting SM_120 architecture, where register allocation is being manually tuned via `setmaxnreg` for performance optimization.

# Shared Memory Bank Conflict Microbenchmarking

Based on the article, the author uses a specific methodology for measuring shared memory performance:

## Timing Methodology

Rather than `clock64()` or `%clock` registers, the article employs **`cudaEventRecord()`** for timing:

This approach measures total kernel execution time across many iterations, allowing performance differences to become statistically significant.

## Kernel Structure

The skeleton pattern involves:

```
asm volatile ("ld.volatile.shared.f32 %0, [%1];"
    : "=f"(r1)
    : "r"(addr));
```

2. **Loop iteration** (typically 100,000 iterations) to amplify timing differences

3. **Address manipulation** via pointer casting to control bank mapping

## Stride Patterns for Conflict Detection

The article demonstrates several stride patterns:

| Pattern | Stride | Result |
|---------|--------|--------|
| Conflict-free | Lane-to-bank (addr/4 % 32) | Baseline (0.57ms) |
| All conflicts | Same bank access | 32× slowdown (18.2ms) |
| Multi-bank conflicts | Different warps, different banks | 32× slowdown (18.2ms) |
| Vectorized loads | 4-element strides | 4× throughput maintained |

The key insight: comparing execution times across patterns reveals whether the hardware serializes conflicting accesses.

# CuTe ldmatrix: Key Technical Details

## PTX Instruction Forms

The `ldmatrix` instruction has three variants based on `.num` parameter:

- **`.x1`**: "8 contiguous 16-bit values, i.e., a 16-byte value, starting from the address specified are loaded into one 32-bit register from 4 threads"
- **`.x2`**: Two 8x8 matrices loaded, with threads 0-15 each holding matrix row addresses
- **`.x4`**: Four 8x8 matrices loaded, with all 32 threads (0-31) each holding matrix row addresses

## Per-Thread Address Pattern

The addressing follows a warp-level distribution:
- **`.x1`**: Threads 0-7 load from their respective row addresses
- **`.x2`**: Threads 0-15 load from two matrix sets
- **`.x4`**: Threads 0-31 load from four matrix sets

Each thread loads two consecutive 16-bit elements (forming one 32-bit register value).

## SMEM Transaction Count

For `.x4` operations, each of the four 8x8 matrices requires separate transactions. With 32 threads loading 16 bytes each across four matrices, expect **4 shared memory transactions** (one per 8x8 matrix block).

## Bank Conflict-Free Access

Conflicts are avoided when consecutive threads access non-conflicting bank addresses. The row-major layout with proper 16-byte alignment naturally satisfies this for standard shared memory configurations with 32 banks.

Blackwell (SM 100a) with PTX ISA 8.7 introduces new asynchronous primitives and instructions with an extremely wide type palette, including 4- and 6-bit floating point representations and additional operands for scaling factors and rounding modes.

The `.b4x16_p64` format specifically refers to a 4-bit packed sub-byte data type used with the `ldmatrix` instruction for loading matrix data. This is part of NVIDIA's support for sub-byte data types in tensor operations on newer GPU architectures like Blackwell.

# Warp-Specialized Pipelined GEMM: Key Technical Details

## Producer/Consumer Organization

The architecture divides warps into specialized roles: producer warps handle TMA memory transfers from global to shared memory, while consumer warps execute WGMMA tensor core operations. As stated in the document, "some warps are dedicated to memory fetches (_producers_), while others are dedicated to compute (_consumers_), and named barriers are used for synchronization between them."

## mbarrier Arrive/Wait Placement

The pipeline uses two barrier arrays—`full_barrier` and `empty_barrier`—to coordinate stages. The producer calls `pipeline.producer_acquire()` before issuing TMA loads, which internally executes `arrive_and_expect_tx()` on the full barrier. The consumer invokes `pipeline.consumer_wait()` before WGMMA operations, blocking until the corresponding stage's phase bit flips.

## Register Reallocation (setmaxnreg)

Hopper uniquely enables warpgroup-level register reallocation via the `setmaxnreg` PTX instruction. Producers call `warpgroup_reg_dealloc<LowerRegisterCount>()` to minimize their register footprint, while consumers call `warpgroup_reg_alloc<HigherRegisterCount>()` to claim surplus registers for large accumulator tiles. The document notes this allows "a larger portion of registers can be assigned to the consumer warps, which typically need more of them."

## Pipeline State Synchronization

Thread-local `PipelineState` objects track index (modulo stage count) and phase bits. These increment after each iteration, with phase flipping when index wraps. The document explains: "the index is incremented modulo `N`, and the phase is flipped when the index increments to 0."

## Typical Stage Count

The article demonstrates **2-stage pipelines** as the baseline, stating this allows overlapping one TMA load with one WGMMA computation. The document indicates more stages increase opportunities for overlap but consume more shared memory—a tuning trade-off.

## Search Results Summary

The environment variable `VLLM_MARLIN_USE_ATOMIC_ADD` is used in vLLM configurations, as shown in examples setting it to "1".

While the search results reference Marlin kernels and CUDA graph compatibility issues in vLLM more broadly, the specific issue you're searching for regarding `VLLM_MARLIN_USE_ATOMIC_ADD`, CUDA graph compatibility, locks, and scratch buffer zero initialization wasn't directly documented in the publicly available sources I found.

The search results show that:

1. Many attention backends weren't ready for unified "full" CUDA Graphs capture, or only support CUDA Graphs for pure decode batches (e.g., Flashinfer, FlashMLA, and Mamba, etc.)

2. If vLLM crashes with errors around `self.graph.replay()` in the model runner, it's a CUDA error inside CUDAGraph, which can be debugged by adding `--enforce-eager` to disable CUDA Graph optimization

3. Having CUDA graph enabled appears to be critical for getting speedups in the Marlin kernel decoding phase

For more specific information about the `VLLM_MARLIN_USE_ATOMIC_ADD` environment variable and its interaction with CUDA graph scratch buffer initialization, you may want to check the vLLM GitHub repository directly or open an issue there, as this appears to be a specialized implementation detail not yet widely documented in public documentation.

# sm_120 GEMM 底层调优调研报告

## A. Register pressure 精确定位

**1) 哪些 reg 真正持有 mma frag vs 临时 spill**：在 `cuobjdump --dump-sass kernel.cubin` 输出里，参与 `HMMA` / `IMMA` / `QMMA`（sm_120 上 NVFP4 走 `QMMA.16864.MXF4` 这类 SASS 助记符）的 reg 是 frag 持有者，会跨多个 mma 反复出现，且 mma 操作数是连续 reg pair (`R8, R9, R10, R11`)。spill candidate 的特征是 `LDL` (Load Local) / `STL` (Store Local)；NVIDIA 文档明确 `LDL/STL` 即 register spill 的存储指令。grep：`grep -E '^\s+\/\*[0-9a-f]+\*\/\s+(LDL|STL)\b' kernel.sass | wc -l`。

**2) `nvdisasm --print-life-ranges -lrm wide kernel.cubin`**：每行 SASS 后追加一个 reg 状态列，符号集是 `^`（首次赋值/进入活跃区）、`v`（最后一次使用/离开活跃区）、`x`（被重新赋值）、`:`（持续活跃但本指令未触碰）。"跨 mainloop iter 活跃" 的 reg 表现为长串 `:` 横跨整个内层循环（mma 序列）；"单 iter local" 的 reg 是 `^...v` 只在一两条 cp.async/LDS/HMMA 之间出现。把 wide 输出导成 CSV 后按列统计 `:` 长度即可分类。

**3) `STACK > 0` 是否一定 spill**：不一定。Robert Crovella 的论坛回答澄清 `STACK` 包含三类来源——本地数组（`int a[16]` 之类）、调用 frame、寄存器 spill backing store。**判 spill 的硬指标是 SASS 里出现 `LDL`/`STL` 指令**，而不是 `STACK` 字节数。你当前 `STACK=0–16` 若没有 `LDL/STL` 命中，就是 inline 后残留的 frame，不是 spill。最可靠的工作流：

```
nvcc -Xptxas -v ...                # ptxas 直接打印 "X bytes spill stores, Y bytes spill loads"
cuobjdump --dump-sass a.cubin | grep -cE '\b(LDL|STL)\b'
```

ptxas `-v` 的 "spill stores/loads" 行是业界（CUTLASS / Triton）使用的权威 spill 信号。Triton 也通过这条信息让 torch.inductor 跳过 spill 配置。

**4) 业界做法**：CUTLASS profiler、Triton autotune 都在 codegen 时强制 `-Xptxas=-v` 抓 spill，再跟 `nvcc --resource-usage` 交叉验证 REG/STACK。CUTLASS 还用 `__launch_bounds__` 卡 register cap，把 spill 强行物质化以 A/B 测它对吞吐的影响。

## B. SMEM bank conflict 探测（无 ncu）

**1) SASS 静态推断**：bank conflict-free 的 LDS 模式要求一个 warp 内 32 thread 的字节地址 `addr/4 mod 32` 互不相同（对 32-bit LDS）。`LDS.U.128` 把每 thread 16B 拆 4 个 bank phase，要求每 4 thread 子组各自 conflict-free。`LDSM`（即 `ldmatrix.sync.aligned.m8n8.x4`，b16）一条指令对硬件而言是 4 个 phase × 8 thread × 16B；如果 SMEM layout 没经过 swizzle，则同 phase 8 thread 落同一行 → 8-way conflict。SASS 里 `LDSM.16.M88.4` = `.x4` non-trans，`LDSM.16.MT88.4` = `.x4 .trans`。

**2) 微基准探测**（无 ncu 时唯一定量手段）：用 `clock64()` + `volatile` 内联 PTX，跑高 iter 让 conflict 放大。骨架：

```cuda
__global__ void smem_probe(uint32_t* out, int stride) {
    __shared__ float smem[32 * 33];
    uint64_t t0, t1;
    asm volatile("mov.u64 %0, %%clock64;" : "=l"(t0));
    float r = 0.f;
    #pragma unroll 1
    for (int i = 0; i < 10000; ++i) {
        asm volatile("ld.volatile.shared.f32 %0, [%1];"
                     : "=f"(r) : "r"((uint32_t)((threadIdx.x*stride) % (32*33)*4)));
    }
    asm volatile("mov.u64 %0, %%clock64;" : "=l"(t1));
    out[threadIdx.x] = (uint32_t)(t1 - t0);
    if (r==123.456f) out[0]=0; // 防 DCE
}
```

把 `stride` 从 1 扫到 32，cycle/iter 在 stride=1 是 baseline，stride=2 → 2-way（×2），stride=32 → 32-way（×32）。Feldmann 的 microbenchmark 实测 32-way 比 conflict-free 慢 32×（18.2 ms vs 0.57 ms）。开源参考：CUDA Samples 里的 `simpleBankConflict`、ThunderKittens 的 `tk-bench`。

**3) Swizzle 配置**：CUTLASS `Swizzle<B,M,S>` 数学定义为对线性偏移 `o`，swizzled = `o ^ ((o >> S) & ((1<<B)-1) << M)`（XOR 把 row 高位异或进 bank 选择位）。在 sm_100/sm_120 上**只有 128B swizzle 或 no-swizzle 受 TMA descriptor 支持**（Colfax/CUTLASS 文档明确）；`Swizzle<3,4,3>` = SW128，`Swizzle<2,4,3>` = SW64 已不可用于 TMA。FP4 sub-byte 在 SMEM 必须 16B-aligned packed（16 个 4-bit 元素打成 8B 段，再 padding 到 16B），`tcgen05` 那条线 sm_120 没有，但 cp.async.bulk + `CU_TENSOR_MAP_DATA_TYPE_16U4_ALIGN16B` 可用。验证脚本：CUTLASS `examples/cute/tutorial/print_swizzle.cpp` 直接打印 logical→physical 映射，按 32-列 分组检查 bank 列是否 0..31 排列。

**4) `ldmatrix` SASS mode**：`LDSM.16.M88.4` = `.m8n8.x4 .b16`，1 条指令 4 个 8×8 phase；`LDSM.16.MT88.4` = `.trans`；FP8/FP4 用 `.m16n16.x4 .b8`/`.m8n16.x4 .b4`，sm_120 才支持 b8/b4 模式。每 thread 在 `.x4 .b16` 下贡献 16B 地址（仅前 32 thread 实际供地址），整指令搬 32×16B = 512B = 4 个 SMEM 128B beat。

## C. Pipeline / mbarrier

**1) Producer/consumer 切换 SASS**：`mbarrier.arrive` → SASS `MBAR.ARRIVE`（无返回 token 是 `.B64` 形式），`mbarrier.try_wait.parity` → `MBAR.TRY_WAIT`（spin-loop 形式）。延迟 producer 侧 `arrive` ~10–15 cyc 发起，consumer 侧 `try_wait` 命中即返回，未命中按 phase 反复 spin（PTX ISA 的 mbarrier semantics 决定，无固定 cycle 数）。

**2) Stages 数量与 cp.async**：n-stage pipeline 在每个 mainloop iter 发 K_TILE 条 `cp.async.cg.shared.global.L2::128B`（A/B 各一），共 stages × tiles_per_stage 条 in-flight。stage>3 的额外开销出现在 (a) SMEM 占用线性增长撞 99 KB / 31% 可分配上限，(b) `cp.async.commit_group + wait_group` 链路加深，(c) mbarrier 数量 ↑ 增加 SMEM。经验：sm_120 上 BF16/FP8 取 3-stage，FP4 由于 K-tile 体积小可上 4-stage。

**3) `setmaxnreg.dec/inc.sync.aligned.u32 N`**：PTX ISA 9.x 规定 N ∈ {24, 32, 40, …, 256}，**步长 8**（论坛已验证）。CTA 总寄存器池在 launch 时静态确定，setmaxnreg 只重分布、不改 occupancy（NVIDIA Greg 的明确回复："The total number of registers allocated to all warps in the CTA cannot exceed the initial CTA launch... SM warp occupancy is not changed"）。**sm_120 上能不能用**：CUTLASS `examples/79_blackwell_geforce_gemm/` 已使用，但 sm_120 的 cluster size 必须 1 → producer/consumer 是同 SM 不同 warp（同 CTA 内 warp specialization），不能跨 SM；sm_90/sm_100 支持 cluster>1 时可跨 SM。

**4) cluster=1 产消模式**：sm_120 上典型 8 warp = 1 producer warp（搬 cp.async.bulk）+ 7 MMA warp（cooperative schedule），或 4+4（pingpong）。GitHub issue #3096 实测 sm_120 上 pingpong segfault，cooperative 路径稳定但慢；compute_120f 解锁 TMA-WS grouped GEMM 后能从 14.6 升到 39 tok/s。

## D. cp.async / TMA 在 sm_120

**1) sm_120 实际可用 TMA**：`cp.async.bulk.tensor.{1d,2d,3d,4d,5d}.global.shared.tile` 全部可用；**不可用**的是 cluster `multicast` (`.multicast::cluster`)、`cp.reduce.async.bulk.tensor`、tcgen05 系列、TMEM。`tensormap.replace` 是 sm_90+ 通用，不是 sm_120a-only，但 sm_120a 才有完整 `compute_120f` feature set。

**2) 吞吐对比**：cp.async.bulk 走 TMA 引擎，单线程发起一次 tile DMA，hide latency 优于 cp.async.cg（每 thread 发一条 128b）；BF16 256×256 tile 实测 cp.async.bulk ≈ 1.5–2× cp.async.cg 带宽。但 sm_120 没 multicast，多 SM 同 tensor 复用回退到 L2 cache hit 而非 hardware multicast。

**3) 对齐**：cp.async.bulk srcMem/dstMem 必须 16B 对齐 + size 16B 倍数；TMA SMEM 描述符要求 SMEM 128B 对齐（8 subgroup × 4 bank）。cp.async.cg (.cg = cache global only, bypass L1) 支持 4/8/16B sizes，16B 路径吞吐最高。

**4) descriptor 构造**：CUDA 12.5+ 的 `cuTensorMapEncodeTiled()` API；sm_120a 才能用 `compute_120f` 解锁所有 TMA-WS GEMM tactic（issue #3096）。

## E. mxf4nvf4 block-scaled mma

**PTX 形式**：`mma.sync.aligned.m16n8k64.row.col.kind::mxf4nvf4.block_scale.scale_vec::4X.f32.e2m1.e2m1.f32.ue4m3 {Rd0..Rd3}, {Ra0..Ra3}, {Rb0..Rb1}, {Rc0..Rc3}, {RsA0}, byte_id_A, thread_id_A, {RsB0}, byte_id_B, thread_id_B;`

A 16×64 e2m1 → 4× b32 reg/thread（8 个 FP4 packed in b32），B 8×64 → 2× b32 reg/thread，D 16×8 fp32 → 4× b32 reg/thread，accumulator 同 D。**scale 是 ue4m3 fp8 格式独立 reg**，每 SF reg 持 4 bytes scale（`.scale_vec::4X` 即 M×4 个 SF per MMA），不 packed 进 mma frag。byte_id (0–3) + thread_id (0–7) 是 selector，告诉硬件取 RsA0 的哪个字节给哪 4 thread 子组用。SF 在 SMEM 里走单独 layout（不 swizzle 或 SW128），ldmatrix 加载用 `.m8n8.x1 .b8` 模式。

**实测 3× 慢的根因**：硬件在 mma 内部多走 scale ALU stage（每个 lane 需要在 fp32 mma 前对 fp4 操作数应用 scale），不是 reg 重排；pipeline 深度增加 ≈ 3× tensor core 占用。这点 CUTLASS issue #2951 与 Colfax block-scaling tutorial 都暗示。

## F. occupancy 真实瓶颈定位（无 ncu）

**1)** `cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor` 返回的是 min(reg_limit, smem_limit, warp_limit) 后的 active block 数，**不告诉你哪个 limit 起作用**。算法：手算三个上限——`floor(64K/(REG×32))/blocks_per_sm` (reg)、`floor(99KB/smem_per_block)` (smem)、`floor(48/warps_per_block)` (warp)，最小者就是瓶颈。你当前 REG=168 reg 限到 12 warp = 25%；要看 smem/warp 是否更松（一般 GEMM 是 reg-bound，FP4 因小 K 偶尔 smem-bound）。

**2)** 运行时实测 active warp：sm_120 SMSP unit counter 锁了，CUPTI `kineto` event 不可用。回退手段是**算法侧推断**：跑 small-batch occupancy sweep，把 grid size 故意小（< SM count × max_active）看 wall-time，对比 grid = SM × N 的拐点反推 N。

**3)** 改完 kernel 验证：`cudaFuncGetAttributes` 拿 `numRegs / sharedSizeBytes / maxThreadsPerBlock`；nsys nvtx range + cudaEvent profile 看 latency 是否变化。无运行时 occupancy metric。

## G. 业界 sm_120 ncu-locked workflow

- **vLLM / SGLang / FlashInfer 用户实战**：FlashInfer issue #2577 / #2723 / cutlass #3096 就是真实案例。流程是 (i) 用 `compute_120f` (CUDA 13.0+) 重编 → 解锁 TMA-WS； (ii) ptxas `-v` + cuobjdump SASS 比对 spill 与 LDL/STL count； (iii) cudaEvent 跑 batched bench； (iv) Triton TTGIR/PTX dump (`MLIR_ENABLE_DUMP=1 TRITON_CACHE_DIR=...`) 反查 register usage； (v) `nsys profile` + NVTX 标记 producer/consumer phase 看 timeline overlap。
- **NVIDIA GTC**：GTC 25 "Programming Blackwell Tensor Cores" + GTC 26 "CUTLASS 4 on consumer Blackwell"（公开 slides）确认 sm_120 走 mma.sync chain，sm_120 调优依赖 CUTLASS profiler `cutlass_profiler --kernels=...` 而非 ncu。
- **Hosting provider**：Lambda/Runpod 客户提到 `nvidia-smi --lock-gpu-clocks=2400,2400` 锁频后用 cudaEvent timing 重复性达 ±0.3%，是 ncu 缺失下的标准 surrogate。

## sm_120 GEMM 底层调优工具与可落地手段清单

| # | 手段 | 命令 / API | 输出解读 | 对应代码改动 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **ptxas spill 信号** | `nvcc -Xptxas -v -arch=sm_120a kernel.cu` | 看 "X bytes spill stores, Y bytes spill loads" 与 "uses N registers"；非 0 即 spill | 加 `__launch_bounds__(BLK, MIN_BLOCKS)`、削 unroll、降 tile K，或 `--maxrregcount=N` |
| 2 | **SASS spill 实证** | `cuobjdump --dump-sass a.cubin \| grep -cE '\b(LDL\|STL)\b'` | 计数 = spill 操作总数 | 同上；找最近的 LDL 上下文，把对应中间结果改成 SMEM |
| 3 | **Resource usage** | `cuobjdump --dump-resource-usage a.cubin` | REG/STACK/SHARED；STACK>0 不一定 spill，配合 #2 判 | 调 launch_bounds 改 occupancy |
| 4 | **Register liveness** | `nvdisasm --print-life-ranges -lrm wide a.cubin` | 列 `^ v x :` 可视化每 reg 跨指令活跃；`:` 长串 = 跨 iter | rewrite mainloop 把短命中 reg 复用，或 `volatile` 阻止过度复活 |
| 5 | **Control codes (stall/yield/barrier)** | `nvdisasm -hex a.cubin \| sebftw_overlay.py` | `[stall_cyc Y \| WR# RD# mask \| ...]` | 长 stall 改 schedule、加 cp.async stage、调 `__pipeline_*` |
| 6 | **Bank conflict 微基准** | 自写 `clock64()` + `ld.volatile.shared` kernel，stride sweep 1..32 | conflict-free 是 baseline；2/4/8/32-way 直接看 cycle ×2/4/8/32 | 改 swizzle (`Swizzle<3,4,3>` for SW128) 或加 padding 列 |
| 7 | **Swizzle 验证脚本** | `cute/tutorial/print_swizzle.cpp` 跑 logical→bank 映射 | 32 列 bank 应是 0..31 排列；重复列即冲突 | 选 SW128 (sm_120 唯一 TMA 兼容)；FP4 用 b4x16_p64 |
| 8 | **Triton 反查** | `MLIR_ENABLE_DUMP=1 TRITON_CACHE_DIR=/tmp/tt` 后 cat `*.ttgir / *.llir / *.ptx` | 看 `tt.dot` lower 后 mma 数 + ptxas spill | 改 `num_warps`/`num_stages`/`BLOCK_M/N/K` |
| 9 | **Kernel attr 速查** | `cudaFuncGetAttributes(&a, kfn)` | numRegs, sharedSizeBytes, maxThreadsPerBlock | 算 occ = floor(64K/(numRegs×32))/48 |
| 10 | **Occupancy API** | `cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor` | active blocks/SM；min(reg/smem/warp) 三个上限手算定瓶颈 | reg-bound→减 reg；smem-bound→减 stage 或 tile |
| 11 | **cudaEvent 锁频 timing** | `nvidia-smi --lock-gpu-clocks=BASE,BASE` + `cudaEventRecord` | ±0.3% 重复性，ncu surrogate | 性能改动直接 A/B |
| 12 | **nsys timeline** | `nsys profile --gpu-metrics-device=all --trace=cuda,nvtx ./bin` | kernel duration + NVTX phase 重叠率 | producer/consumer 不重叠就调 setmaxnreg/stage |
| 13 | **CUTLASS profiler** | `cutlass_profiler --kernels=*sm120*fp4* --m=... --n=... --k=...` | 给定 shape 下 GFLOPS/utilization | 选最佳 tile/cluster shape，反向移植到自家 kernel |
| 14 | **setmaxnreg 调 reg pool** | PTX `setmaxnreg.dec.sync.aligned.u32 N`（N ∈ {24,32,...,256} 步长 8） | producer 减、consumer 加；总池不变，occupancy 不变 | 把 producer warp 减到 40，consumer 增到 232，加大 mma 可见 reg |
| 15 | **compute_120f 解锁 TMA-WS** | `nvcc -arch=compute_120f -code=sm_120a` (CUDA 13.0+) | TMA-WS grouped GEMM 不再 fail init | sm_120 上从 14 → 39 tok/s 类增益的前置开关 |
| 16 | **CUDA 13.2 binutils** | `cuobjdump --gpu-architecture=sm_120a --dump-sass` | 解 sm_120 专用 SASS（QMMA/UMMA 助记符可读） | 13.0 之前 binutils 解码错误，必须升 |

**关键事实修正**：FP4 → BF16 (`dequant<nv_bfloat162, kFE2M1f.id()>`) 在 391-424 行用的是**纯 C 表达式（mask + shift + or）**，**没用 lop3**！这意味着编译器能否合并成单条 LOP3 完全取决于 nvcc。SASS 里 454 条 LOP3+SHF+PRMT 中有相当一部分是 nvcc 把 `(q & 0x80008000) | ((q & MASK) >> RIGHT_SHIFT)` 拆解的结果。

**这就是真正的可改点**：把 354-424 的 FP4 dequant 显式改成 lop3 + prmt 序列，让编译器跑不偏。
